content: The BPALM/BPAL regimen is recommended for individuals aged 14 years and older. This age threshold is based on the lack of sufficient data to support its use in children under 14 years of age. The regimen is applicable to both adults and adolescents within this age group. HIV status and CD4 count were not exclusion criteria in the TB-PRACTECAL trial, and people living with HIV (PLHIV) accounted for 27% of the enrolled participants. The median CD4 count among PLHIV was 322 cells/mm³, with an interquartile range of 217–622 cells/mm³ across the study arms. Drug–drug interactions must be carefully considered when co-administering TB and HIV medications. While some antiretroviral therapies should be avoided, alternative agents can be used when pretomanid is part of the regimen. The BPALM/BPAL regimen is recommended for all individuals regardless of HIV status, but caution is advised for patients with CD4 counts below 100 cells/mm³. Pregnant and breastfeeding women were excluded from the ZeNix and TB-PRACTECAL trials due to unknown effects of pretomanid on fetal development. Consequently, no specific analysis for this subgroup was conducted. Breastfeeding is not recommended for women taking pretomanid. Therefore, the BPALM/BPAL regimen is not applicable to pregnant or breastfeeding women. In such cases, alternative treatment options should be considered. Patients with extrapulmonary TB were excluded from the ZeNix and TB-PRACTECAL trials, and no specific analysis for this subgroup was performed. Data on the central nervous system (CNS) penetration of bedaquiline and pretomanid are limited. The BPALM/BPAL regimen is recommended for pulmonary TB and most forms of extrapulmonary TB, except for severe cases involving the CNS, osteoarticular TB, or disseminated (miliary) TB, which may require specialized treatment approaches. Certain patient groups were excluded from the trials, including those with liver enzyme levels three times above the upper limit of normal, corrected QT intervals (QTcF) exceeding 500 ms, significant cardiac conditions, severe peripheral neuropathy (Grade 3–4), or very low body mass index (BMI < 17). These patients may only receive the regimen if deemed the best option by the treating physician despite these contraindications. High treatment success rates observed in the Nix-TB, ZeNix, and TB-PRACTECAL trials, along with favorable comparisons to standard-of-care regimens, support the implementation of the BPALM/BPAL regimen under routine programmatic conditions. However, as this recommendation is conditional, ongoing operational research will provide additional insights to refine implementation guidance. Careful patient selection is critical to replicate the treatment success rates seen in the trials. Eligible patients should have bacteriologically confirmed multidrug-resistant or rifampicin-resistant TB (MDR/RR-TB), with or without fluoroquinolone resistance. Drug susceptibility testing (DST) is essential to assess prior use and susceptibility to the regimen's components. Patients with a history of more than one month of prior use of bedaquiline, pretomanid (or delamanid), or linezolid should not be enrolled unless recent DST confirms susceptibility. Fluoroquinolone resistance testing should also be performed before starting treatment. If fluoroquinolone resistance is confirmed, moxifloxacin should be omitted, and the regimen continued as BPAL only. In the absence of fluoroquinolone resistance, moxifloxacin enhances regimen efficacy and is recommended. DST services must be strengthened globally to support the implementation of MDR/RR-TB treatment regimens. Initial testing for fluoroquinolone resistance can be performed using assays like Xpert® MTB/XDR or GenoType® MTBDRsl. Testing for bedaquiline and linezolid susceptibility is desirable at baseline and during treatment if culture conversion is not achieved. Pretomanid DST methods are under development, and surveillance of resistance to new medicines should be incorporated into routine efforts. Drug–drug interactions must be considered when co-administering TB and HIV medications. For example, efavirenz significantly reduces pretomanid exposure, necessitating alternative antiretroviral agents. Dolutegravir-based regimens combined with two nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors are preferred for co-administration with BPALM/BPAL. Patient support is essential to ensure adherence and optimize treatment outcomes. This can include facilitating visits to healthcare facilities, home visits by healthcare staff, or using digital technologies for daily communication. Active pharmacovigilance, management of adverse drug reactions, and prevention of complications from drug–drug interactions are critical for patient care. Reporting adverse reactions to national drug-safety authorities informs policy decisions. The BPALM/BPAL regimen consists of bedaquiline, pretomanid, and linezolid, with or without moxifloxacin. Pretomanid is administered at 200 mg once daily for the entire regimen duration. Moxifloxacin, if included, is dosed at 400 mg once daily. Bedaquiline dosing schemes vary slightly between trials but are comparable in overall drug exposure. Either daily dosing throughout treatment or a loading dose followed by thrice-weekly dosing may be used. Linezolid dosing in the ZeNix trial was optimized to 600 mg once daily for 26 weeks, with a reduction to 300 mg daily allowed in cases of toxicity. In the TB-PRACTECAL trial, participants received 600 mg daily for 16 weeks, followed by 300 mg daily for the remaining 8 weeks. The preferred approach is 600 mg daily throughout the regimen, with dose reduction to 300 mg if necessary to mitigate toxicity. The BPALM/BPAL regimens have been studied as standardized treatment courses. Modifications, such as early discontinuation or replacement of any component medicines, may lead to suboptimal outcomes. Eligible patients with fluoroquinolone susceptibility can start the BPALM regimen for six months without prolongation unless missed doses need to be compensated.
